orders.trial_court_action: Denied defendants’ motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Walukanis allegedly tripped over an uneven condition near the entrance doors of defendants’ premises. The opinion gives no measurements for the defect.

legal_issues.finding: Considering the physical characteristics and circumstances, defendants did not establish that the uneven condition was trivial as a matter of law.
Since defendants failed to carry their initial burden, the court did not consider the sufficiency of the opposition.

quality.notes: The holding leaves the defect’s actionability open. Neither building use nor title is specified.

evidence.quote: Richard Walukanis et al., Respondents, v Rockville Office Centre Associates et al., Appellants.
the defendants appeal from an order of the Supreme Court, Nassau County (Brown, J.), entered March 12, 2015, which denied their motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
Ordered that the order is affirmed, with costs.
The injured plaintiff allegedly tripped and fell over an uneven condition in the area near the entrance doors of the defendants' premises.
The defendants moved for summary judgment dismissing the complaint, contending that the alleged hazardous condition was trivial and not actionable.

Considering the width, depth, elevation, irregularity, and appearance of the defect, together with the time, place, and circumstance of the injury, it cannot be said as a matter of law that the condition at issue was trivial and therefore not actionable
Since the defendants failed to establish their prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law, it is not necessary to review the sufficiency of the plaintiffs' opposition papers
Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly denied the defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

orders.trial_court_action: Granted defendants’ motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint because the trial court considered causation speculative.

facts.factual_summary: Bovee said his foot struck pavement as he approached the store. He identified two nearby cracks in a photograph of the parking lot and could not say which one stopped his foot.

legal_issues.finding: Defendants did not carry their burden on notice. The co-owner denied earlier complaints but identified the pavement cuts as remnants of the town’s work.
The co-owner’s account and photographs left open whether the condition had been visible and apparent long enough for defendants to discover it.
Even assuming an initial showing of triviality, the engineer’s account of the heave and the surrounding parking-lot conditions left actionability for the jury.
A jury could infer that one of the two cracks caused Bovee’s fall without identifying the precise crack.
The engineer alleged violations of applicable standards and codes; the court did not find a particular provision violated.
Bovee’s engineer inspected the site and described a roughly one-inch heave, linking it to the abrupt stop of Bovee’s foot. His affidavit supported a factual dispute.

evidence_discussed.description: Bovee identified the area of his fall; the co-owner described maintenance, the pavement cuts and the history of complaints.
Bovee circled the area containing two cracks in a photograph. The court also considered the photographs on visibility and notice.
The engineer inspected the pavement, reviewed testimony and photographs, and opined that cracking and heaving created a hazard.

quality.notes: Town utility work is evidence about the origin and age of the cuts; the accident was in the lot of the privately owned store.

evidence.quote: Appeal from an order of the Supreme Court (Crowell, J.), entered June 23, 2021 in Saratoga County, which granted defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
Plaintiff commenced this negligence action seeking damages for injuries that he sustained when he tripped and fell in the parking lot of a store owned by defendants.
Finding that plaintiff's testimony regarding the cause of his fall was speculative, Supreme Court granted the motion.
Plaintiff appeals, and we reverse.

Plaintiff testified that, on the day of the incident, the weather was clear and there was no snow or debris on the surface of the parking lot. He had parked his car in the parking lot and was approaching the front door of the store when his foot suddenly "hit something along the pavement and . . . stopped," causing him to fall to the ground.

Plaintiff was shown photographs of the parking lot and identified the [*2] location of his fall by circling in one of the photographs an uneven area of the pavement with two cracks in close proximity to one another. Upon further questioning, plaintiff was unable to identify which of the two cracks caused the fall, but repeatedly testified that he knew it was one of those two cracks based upon where he landed when he fell.
plaintiff was not required to state for certain which particular crack caused him to fall in order to withstand summary judgment

From plaintiff's testimony, a jury could rationally infer that one of the two cracks in this area of the pavement was the cause of his fall without being forced to resort to mere speculation and surmise
Defendants likewise failed to meet their burden of demonstrating as a matter of law that they did not have actual or constructive notice of the alleged dangerous condition.

Their submissions included the affidavit and examination before trial testimony of Mark Posniewski, the store's co-owner. Posniewski testified that he has maintained the store's parking lot since 2002 and that there were no prior accidents or complaints regarding its condition.

Posniewski testified that the "cuts" in pavement depicted in the various photographs, including those identified by plaintiff as the potential cause of his fall, were from the work performed by the Town.
He also expressed an unawareness as to whether anyone from the Town ever came to inspect the work and testified that the parking lot has not since been repaved or resurfaced [*3] .

Considering Posniewski's testimony and the photographs submitted on the motion, we find that defendants failed to eliminate triable issues of fact as to whether the defect that allegedly caused plaintiff's fall was visible and apparent and existed for a sufficient length of time prior to the accident to permit defendants to have discovered and remedied it

Plaintiff proffered the expert affidavit of a professional engineer who inspected the area of the parking lot where plaintiff fell and reviewed, among other things, the deposition testimony of plaintiff and Posniewski and the photographs of the accident site exchanged during discovery. The expert averred that the area where plaintiff fell is in poor condition due to the presence of multiple cracks and a heave [*4] that raises the height of the pavement approximately one inch above grade.

Based upon plaintiff's description of the accident, the expert opined that the "cracked and heaved" section of the pavement trapped plaintiff's foot and caused his travel to come to a sudden and abrupt stop, resulting in his fall.

The expert further averred that the cracked and heaved section of the parking lot where plaintiff fell violated applicable standards and codes, and opined with a reasonable degree of professional certainty that the defects in the pavement created a dangerous condition that caused plaintiff's fall.
the determination as to whether the defect was so trivial and slight in nature as to be nonactionable should be left for a jury
Ordered that the order is reversed, on the law, with costs, and motion denied.

orders.description: New York County order entered on or about July 10, 2023, upon reargument
orders.trial_court_action: Upon reargument, denied the appealing defendants’ motions for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Molina testified that she tripped on the upturned edges of a Masonite board in a lobby outside the elevator. The opinion describes a dispute about whether Romo moved equipment over the boards and failed to re-tape them.

legal_issues.finding: A factual issue remained whether moving equipment and failing to re-tape the board created the hazard.
Whether Romo’s foreman had seen the hazardous condition during his inspection remained disputed.
The condominium offered no evidence of a pre-fall inspection. Romo made an initial showing through its foreman’s inspection about 40 minutes earlier, but Molina raised triable issues.
Molina identified the upturned edges as causing her trip. The testimony conflicted over whether the board was defective at that time.
On reargument, the court reached the merits. Conflicting testimony about the board required credibility findings at trial.

evidence_discussed.description: Molina testified that the board edges bent upward and caused her to trip.
Romo’s foreman testified that he inspected the area 40 minutes beforehand.

quality.notes: The defendant condominium is named and evaluated on inspection of the lobby, but the opinion does not expressly establish ownership or control of the accident area. The reargument ruling is substantive, and both denials were affirmed.

evidence.quote: Margarita Molina, Respondent, v The Loft 124 Condominium et al., Appellants, et al., Defendant.

Order, Supreme Court, New York County (Shlomo S. Hagler, J.), entered on or about July 10, 2023, which, upon reargument, denied defendants' motions for summary judgment dismissing the complaint, unanimously affirmed, without costs.
The motion court properly denied the appealing defendants' summary judgment motions.
Defendant The Loft 124 Condominium failed to proffer any evidence that it had inspected the alleged defective Masonite board outside the elevator area of the lobby before plaintiff's fall

Defendant Romo Construction Corp. demonstrated its prima facie entitlement to summary judgment through its foreman's testimony that he examined the subject area only 40 minutes before plaintiff's fall
One is whether the foreman had seen the hazardous condition of the Masonite board upon his inspection

The other is whether Romo had created the condition by, among other things, moving equipment over the Masonite boards and failing to properly re-tape it, given that plaintiff testified that the edges of the board were bent upwards causing her to trip and fall

Given the conflicting testimony as to whether the Masonite board was in a defective condition at the time of plaintiff's accident, any determination would be based upon the credibility of the parties, which is to be resolved at trial and not on a motion for summary judgment

orders.trial_court_action: Granted defendants’ motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Sosa allegedly slipped on a piece of cardboard on the floor of defendants’ premises.

legal_issues.finding: The cardboard was readily observable and not inherently dangerous. Sosa did not raise a triable factual issue.
The court rejected Sosa’s challenge to the use of the parties’ deposition transcripts.

evidence_discussed.description: The trial court properly considered transcripts of the parties’ depositions; their specific contents were not supplied.

quality.notes: The opinion identifies the accident as occurring on defendants’ premises without describing the building’s use or Sosa’s role.

evidence.quote: the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Queens County (Sampson, J.), entered December 6, 2011, which granted the defendants’ motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
Ordered that the order is affirmed, with costs.
The plaintiff allegedly slipped and fell on a piece of cardboard that was on the floor of the defendants’ premises.

the defendants established their prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law by demonstrating that the piece of cardboard was not an inherently dangerous condition and was readily observable by the reasonable use of the plaintiff’s senses
Contrary to the plaintiff’s contention, the Supreme Court properly considered the transcripts of the parties’ depositions
In opposition, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact.
Therefore, the Supreme Court properly granted the defendants’ motion.

orders.description: Suffolk County order dated November 13, 2013, in the Insurance Law § 3420 action
orders.trial_court_action: Denied Karl summary judgment on the insurance claim and granted North Country’s cross-motion dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Karl slipped and fell at Crystal Garden on December 22, 2006. The restaurant was owned by the insured restaurant entity. The opinion supplies no particular hazard or location within the premises.

legal_issues.finding: The insurer timely and properly disclaimed coverage because Karl failed to promptly forward the summons and complaint. The appeal concerned recovery of an unsatisfied judgment, not premises liability.

evidence_discussed.description: The insurance policy required prompt forwarding of legal papers; North Country received the papers in June 2008 and disclaimed in July.

quality.notes: North Country was the insurer in the current action. The restaurant default judgment is background, not an independently appealed judgment. Insurance notice is not premises-hazard notice.

evidence.quote: In an action pursuant to Insurance Law § 3420 to recover the amount of an unsatisfied judgment from the defendant, the judgment debtor's insurer, the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Suffolk County (Pastoressa, J.), dated November 13, 2013, which denied his motion for summary judgment on the complaint and granted the defendant's cross motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
Ordered that the order is affirmed, with costs.

On March 31, 2010, a default judgment in favor of the plaintiff was entered against Crystal Garden Chinese Buffet (hereinafter Crystal Garden) and C.Penal Law Restaurant, Inc. (hereinafter the Restaurant), in a personal injury action the plaintiff commenced against Crystal Garden and the Restaurant (hereinafter the underlying action).
The underlying action arose out of an incident that occurred on December 22, 2006, when the plaintiff slipped and fell at Crystal Garden, which is owned by the Restaurant.
The policy required notice of the occurrence to be given to North Country as soon as practicable, and required legal papers to be forwarded promptly.
Neither Crystal Gardens nor the Restaurant satisfied the judgment.
North Country was notified for the first time of the commencement of the underlying action on June 27, 2008, when it received a copy of the summons and complaint from the plaintiff's counsel.
On July 3, 2008, North Country disclaimed coverage based upon the plaintiff's failure to provide timely notice of the occurrence and timely notice of commencement of the lawsuit.
On July 28, 2010, the plaintiff commenced this action against North Country seeking [*2] to recover the amount of the unsatisfied judgment in the underlying action.
North Country made a prima facie showing that it timely and properly disclaimed coverage based upon the plaintiff's failure to promptly forward a copy of the summons and complaint to North Country
In opposition, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact.
Therefore, the Supreme Court properly granted North Country's cross motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint
